opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing that meeting did was turn something that was a bottom-up interest into a company-level commitment. Before that, generative modeling at NVIDIA was mostly researchers like us who were excited about GANs, diffusion and so on, doing projects because we found them interesting. When we wrote to Jensen, we were basically saying: we think this is going to be big, and we want to do it more seriously. He didn't just reply "sounds good." He pulled people together, and that changed the nature of the conversation.

A few things came out of it. First, alignment. When Jensen is in the room, the different groups, research, product, infrastructure, hear the same message at the same time. You don't spend six months persuading each team one by one. Everyone leaves understanding this is a priority.

Second, resources. Generative models, especially as they scale, need a lot of compute and a lot of data engineering. As a research group, you can't get that just by asking nicely. Once leadership says this matters, compute allocation and headcount become much easier conversations.

Third, and maybe most subtle, it set the ambition level. Jensen tends to push you to think about the end state, not the next paper. The question shifted from "can we publish a nice result" to "what would it take to build a foundation model that people actually use, and what does that mean for the whole computing stack?" That framing pushed us toward thinking about world models and physical AI, models that understand the physical world, which connects naturally to robotics and autonomous driving, things NVIDIA cares about.

So I wouldn't say the meeting produced a specific technical decision. What it accomplished was legitimacy and focus. It told everyone this isn't a side project anymore. In a big company, that signal is often the hardest part, and once you have it, the technical work can actually move fast.

r001.rationale: The response describes the meeting as creating company-level commitment, alignment, resources, and focus from bottom-up interest. It explicitly says the meeting produced no specific technical decision and does not characterize it as turning an already established consensus into a concrete execution plan.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest thing it accomplished was that it stopped us from running in several different directions at once. Before that email, a few of us in NVIDIA Research were each poking at generative models in our own corners. Some people were doing GANs for images, some were working on video, some on 3D, and we all sensed this was about to become something much bigger than a research curiosity. So we wrote to Jensen basically saying, we think this is going to matter for the company, and we don't want to be late.

What surprised me about the meeting was that he didn't treat it as a research update. He treated it as a business question. He kept asking, if this works, what does it change for NVIDIA? Not just what paper comes out of it, but who buys more GPUs, what products get built, what does the platform need to look like. That reframing was really the accomplishment. It forced us to connect the research to a thesis about where the whole industry was going.

The second thing it did was give us permission to be ambitious about scale. In research you tend to be careful about compute, you write proposals for a handful of GPUs. He made it clear that if we believed in it, we should think about it at a scale that actually tests the idea. That mattered a lot for what became our later work, because generative models really do live or die on data and compute.

And the third thing, which sounds small but isn't, is that it put people in the same room who normally wouldn't talk. Research, product, the platform teams. After that meeting there was a shared understanding that generative AI wasn't one group's project. It was something the company was going to organize around.

So I'd say it didn't produce a single decision that day. It produced alignment, and alignment at NVIDIA tends to move very fast once Jensen is personally interested.

r001.rationale: The response describes the meeting as creating alignment and encouraging ambition, but says it produced no single decision. It does not characterize the meeting as turning an existing consensus into a concrete execution plan.

astra-6.text: I think the main thing it accomplished was turning an idea we had emailed him about into a conversation about whether we should pursue it. There’s a difference between a group being excited about generative models and having a shared sense of what to do next. To me, that was the value of the meeting: getting the idea serious attention and creating an opportunity to align on a direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes the meeting as opening a discussion about whether to pursue the idea and aligning on direction. It does not say there was already consensus or that the meeting produced a concrete execution plan.

sol-6.1.text: I think the main thing it accomplished was alignment. An email can convey an idea, but a meeting lets you discuss why it matters, what the uncertainties are, and what it would take to pursue it. I wouldn’t say the meeting itself solved the technical problems. Its value was getting everyone focused on whether this was a direction worth taking seriously.
